Attribution: Netflix TechBlog [platforms_infrastructure] https://netflixtechblog.com/fact-checking-at-scale-building-a-more-accurate-and-efficient-synopsis-factuality-system-d7d85859d808?source=rss----2615bd06b42e---4

By Shreya S Ramanujam, Yongce Li, Afshine Amidi, Sina Ghiassian, Benjamin Klein. Introduction Picture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen: If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode. A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in. But of course, we can’t just write anything. “In the fog-drenched streets of Victorian London, Detective Daphne Bridgerton races to unmask a serial killer known only as the elusive Lady Whistledown.” Intriguing? Definitely. But it is most certainly not the premise of Bridgerton.

### Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache and weight transfer for inference and RL on TPU
Source: Google Cloud Blog
Published: 2026-11-09 13:00 UTC
URL: https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/ai-infrastructure/introducing-tpu-sync-fast-kv-cache-and-weight-transfer-on-tpu/
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Google Cloud Blog [platforms_infrastructure] https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/ai-infrastructure/introducing-tpu-sync-fast-kv-cache-and-weight-transfer-on-tpu/

As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers to rollout samplers during RL. Whenever this state is trapped inside a single chip's memory or stalled on network transfers, AI accelerators sit idle. We designed TPU Sync from first principles to serve as the model-state layer across TPU clusters — built on the architectural insight that accelerator High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network (DCN) should operate as a single, co-designed memory hierarchy. An open-source, native C++ library, TPU Sync moves TPU-tiled tensors directly across this hierarchy with asynchronous DMA transfers that overlap data movement with active computation.

### Now generally available: GKE dynamic slicing for higher resilience, and efficiency for TPUs
Source: Google Cloud Blog
Published: 2026-11-09 13:00 UTC
URL: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/containers-kubernetes/gke-dynamic-slicing-on-tpus/
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Google Cloud Blog [platforms_infrastructure] https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/containers-kubernetes/gke-dynamic-slicing-on-tpus/

Running large-scale AI workloads on TPU and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) requires infrastructure that adapts as fast as your models change. Dynamic Slicing is generally available on GKE, which decouples logical TPU slice formation from physical nodepool provisioning. Compared to creating a static nodepool for each TPU slice, dynamic slicing reduces AI workload startup times by up to 5x and workload recovery by 4.5x — maximizing TPU goodput, efficiency, and workload resilience at scale. Beyond one workload, one nodepool Previously, managing TPU capacity at GKE standard required separate, fixed TPU slice topology nodepools, increasing startup times and complexity while preventing multi-host nodepools from hosting multiple AI workloads. Changing workload needs meant manually deleting and recreating nodepools. Additionally, this tight coupling created large failure domains where a single hardware fault crashed an entire slice, slowing recovery while reprovisioning.

The Workflow SDK now sends event writes and stream writes to Vercel Workflows over a WebSocket by default, replacing one HTTP request per write, or per write group for streams. No code change is needed beyond upgrading to workflow@5.2.0 or later. Once you deploy the upgrade, new runs use it. In-flight runs finish on the deployment they started on. Existing streaming code works as is. A step that writes a burst of chunks, like AI tokens, sends them over the WebSocket once it opens: Streams keep pace with AI output In a benchmark replaying an AI agent's token stream, v5.2.0, which writes streams over a WebSocket by default, delivered the full response 4.2× faster than v4.8.12, with no chunk delayed over a second. Fewer HTTP requests for event writes Every step start and completion is an event write, now sent over the WebSocket, so workflows with many steps make fewer HTTP requests. The added efficiency also improves performance and reduces costs. The queue handler opens the connection for every delivery. Get started Read the Vercel World documentation to get started. Vercel Container Registry now supports compressed image layers of up to 2 GB each, up from 500 MB, the total image size limit stays 15 GB. The registry works with standard workflows like docker push, docker pull, and docker tag, and pushing an image creates the repository on the fly. Repositories can be made public for read-only pull access by any Vercel team, or shared with specific teams up to 100 from the dashboard or with vercel vcr permissions. The Vercel Managed Images that Vercel Sandbox runs on are served from ordinary public repositories, built with the same public-repository feature any team can use for its own images. Manage repositories, images, and tags with the vercel vcr CLI commands in Vercel CLI v58.3.0 or later, and log CI workflows in from GitHub Actions with the vercel/vcr-action/login action using GitHub OIDC, which removes the need for long-lived registry credentials. If background optimization of a pushed image fails, the image shows an error status in the dashboard, and pushing the same image again retries the conversion.

### Announcing the Workload Conformance Working Group
Source: Kubernetes Blog
Published: 2026-10-27 04:30 UTC
URL: https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/10/27/announcing-workload-conformance-wg/
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Kubernetes Blog [platforms_infrastructure] https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/10/27/announcing-workload-conformance-wg/

We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group. The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on. Why workloads need a shared standard Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version. Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use. Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions.

By Praneeth Yenugutala, Victor Dusa, Anastasia Samoilova, Megan Ren, Justin Wei, Marcelo Mayworm At Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines. Our first answer to that problem was Pensive, an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro. It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic.

Attribution: Netflix TechBlog [platforms_infrastructure] https://netflixtechblog.com/beyond-api-compatibility-building-a-tool-to-measure-the-blast-radius-of-library-changes-9474f2fd4f90?source=rss----2615bd06b42e---4

By Roberto Perez Alcolea, Java Platform Team Quasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decision At Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed. The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it. Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.

Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years. For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run.

### Why Is My Kubernetes Job Still Pending? Tracing Kueue Admission with Headlamp
Source: Kubernetes Blog
Published: 2026-10-14 18:35 UTC
URL: https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/10/14/tracing-kueue-admission-with-headlamp/
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Kubernetes Blog [platforms_infrastructure] https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/10/14/tracing-kueue-admission-with-headlamp/

You submit a Kubernetes Job and wait for its Pods to appear. A minute passes. Then another. The Job is still suspended, there are no application logs, and there may not even be a Pod to inspect. In a cluster managed by Kueue, this can be completely normal. Kueue may still be deciding whether the Job can use the requested resources. The useful question is not only “Why is the Pod pending?” It is first “Has Kueue admitted the Workload?” The Kueue plugin for Headlamp brings that investigation into the Headlamp UI. Instead of reconstructing the admission path from several commands and large YAML objects, you can begin with the Workload, read its condition message, and follow links through the LocalQueue, ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Cohort. This article follows that Headlamp-first path. The command line appears only in a short optional section for reproducing the example. Before you begin You need a Kubernetes cluster with Kueue installed, a Headlamp installation, and the 0.1.0-alpha Kueue plugin.

### The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know
Source: Kubernetes Blog
Published: 2026-10-06 18:00 UTC
URL: https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/10/06/kubernetes-cgroups-v2-shift/
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Kubernetes Blog [platforms_infrastructure] https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/10/06/kubernetes-cgroups-v2-shift/

In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode. Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1 Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1. Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true, so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file, but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy. Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support. If you are still on a release older than v1.

### Scaling Kubernetes Workloads with Node Swap
Source: Kubernetes Blog
Published: 2026-10-05 18:00 UTC
URL: https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/10/05/scaling-kubernetes-workloads-with-node-swap/
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Kubernetes Blog [platforms_infrastructure] https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/10/05/scaling-kubernetes-workloads-with-node-swap/

Memory is often the first hard limit a Kubernetes cluster hits. Nodes run out of RAM long before they run out of CPU, and the new wave of agentic AI workloads makes this worse. These workloads demand large memory footprints to start up and run untrusted code, then sit idle waiting for the next prompt. That idle but resident memory is expensive, and it caps how many pods a node can hold. This is where swap helps. Kubernetes support for running nodes with swap enabled reached General Availability in v1.34, and by backing that swap with fast NVMe solid state drives (SSDs), a node can page out dormant memory and pack in far more pods. This post explains how we benchmarked that approach across three workloads, including CI/CD kernel builds, sandboxed headless browsers, and isolated Python runtimes; we found density gains of up to 3×, often with little or no latency cost.

As Kubernetes adoption has grown, the conversation has shifted beyond running containers to managing increasingly complex application lifecycles. Modern platforms support stateless web services, stateful databases, batch processing, AI workloads, and platform services. At the same time, they must remain reliable during upgrades, scaling events, and infrastructure failures. Every Kubernetes user relies on SIG Apps, whether they realize it or not. Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, and CronJobs form the foundation of how applications are deployed, updated, scaled, and operated across the Kubernetes ecosystem. SIG Apps is focused on improving workload resilience, refining application lifecycle management, and addressing the operational challenges that emerge when applications encounter node failures, rollout disruptions, and increasingly complex infrastructure environments.

### Can Agentic Robotics Solve Robotics’ Data Scaling Problem?
Source: IEEE Spectrum Robotics
Published: 2026-11-09 14:00 UTC
URL: https://spectrum.ieee.org/agentic-robotics
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: IEEE Spectrum Robotics [cybernetics_automation] https://spectrum.ieee.org/agentic-robotics

Robotics companies are investing heavily in the belief that data will solve the most difficult problems in robotics. Once AI systems have ingested enough data from human demonstrations, the thinking goes, robots will be able to perform the vast majority of the manual tasks that humans now do. There are even robotics companies that exist solely to collect training data and sell it to other robotics companies in pursuit of this goal. But whether data will finally bring us general-purpose robots is an open question. Nobody knows how much data would be necessary, what kind of data is important, or whether something else might be missing. And there are other problems with a reliance on massive amounts of data: the resulting AI algorithms are essentially black boxes, which despite their high performance are difficult or impossible for humans to understand. This characteristic is becoming increasingly concerning in commercial deployments, where robots must be flexible, reliable, and safe.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute. NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos. This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing. A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse. In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out. “It will.

Rick and Marcia LeCompte loved to watch the Cooper’s hawks that frequented a sweet-gum tree in their yard in Baton Rouge, La. But this October, the hawks were gone. Marcia LeCompte is convinced the birds were scared away by the same flying robots that have been vexing the couple since early September. The noise had them spending less time outside in their garden, and even inside their home, they couldn’t escape the near-constant buzzing. Angry and feeling harassed, the LeComptes began to think about moving. The problem: delivery drones. Amazon’s MK30 delivery drones are large and must fly near the ground when making deliveries.Annabel Lee-Ellis/Press Association/AP Images Last August, Amazon Prime Air began flying its MK30 drones from a distribution center 3.2 kilometers (2 miles) from the LeComptes’ home. People in the neighborhood first noticed just a few of the drones, flying high (U.S. regulations authorize drones to fly at up to 120 meters (400 feet)). But a couple of weeks later, they felt as if drones were everywhere, and often flying much lower.

Inspecting thousands of kilometers of power lines, pipelines, or rail tracks is an expensive and time-consuming business. It’s typically done by helicopters, which are costly, noisy, and polluting. French startup HyLight thinks uncrewed airships could be a cheaper, more environmentally friendly alternative. The company has developed a 12-meter-long blimp powered by a hydrogen fuel cell capable of staying airborne for up to 10 hours and traveling 350 kilometers per day. The airship carries an array of sensors for inspection, including high-precision cameras, lidar, and methane detectors. HyLight uses AI models (some developed in-house, some off the shelf) to automatically analyze collected data and identify more than 50 types of maintenance issues. The French civil aviation authority and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency have both granted permission for HyLight’s airships—which have so far logged more than 750 flight hours—to operate beyond visual line of sight.

In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward. At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration. Within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left. Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right.

The skies are becoming dangerously crowded—not with planes but with interference and jamming disrupting many of the 30,000 radio frequencies that civil aviation relies upon. In previous decades, designers of aviation weather, navigation, and voice communication systems prioritized convenience over security, leaving today’s aircraft vulnerable to both unwitting interference and malicious jamming and spoofing, especially near conflict zones. Driven by growing threats and a critical U.S. Government Accountability Office report, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is now seeking ambitious monitoring and detection systems to protect its spectrum nationwide. At an industry engagement day in mid-October, the FAA’s vice president of technical operations, Dan Murphy, laid out the problem: “Right now, somewhere in the National Airspace System, a signal that aviation depends upon is being jammed, being spoofed, or just being degraded by something else happening in the spectrum.

Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline

This article is brought to you by VicOne. A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal. But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path. In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation. At VicOne LAB R7, we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe. How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behavior A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions.

In a lab in Luxembourg in 2024, engineers at Flawless Photonics unpacked a spool of glass fiber that had just returned from the International Space Station (ISS). As they threaded it onto their rewinding machine, the machine jammed—as happens sometimes—and they braced for the usual outcome: The fiber would snap. This time, though, nothing broke. It was an early hint that their experiment might have been successful. The Flawless Photonics team had set out to draw fibers of a heavy-metal fluoride glass called ZBLAN—named for its other components of zirconium, barium, lanthanum, aluminum, and sodium (chemical symbol Na)—in microgravity, aiming to achieve superior optical and physical properties. “We realized, wow, that fiber is much stronger than the stuff we had produced on Earth,” says Hubert Moser, the company’s cofounder and CTO. ZBLAN Fiber’s Microgravity Advantages Photonics engineers have been intrigued by ZBLAN for decades because it can, in theory, transmit light with 1 percent of the loss of silica.

Attribution: IEEE Spectrum [hardware_radio_embedded] https://spectrum.ieee.org/zero-trust-agentic-ai-architecture

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast. Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

### How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?
Source: IEEE Spectrum Aerospace / IEEE Spectrum
Published: 2026-11-06 15:00 UTC
URL: https://spectrum.ieee.org/mmx-mission-to-phobos
Source meta: IEEE Spectrum Aerospace [cybernetics_automation]: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline | IEEE Spectrum [hardware_radio_embedded]: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: IEEE Spectrum Aerospace [cybernetics_automation] https://spectrum.ieee.org/mmx-mission-to-phobos
Attribution: IEEE Spectrum [hardware_radio_embedded] https://spectrum.ieee.org/mmx-mission-to-phobos

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute. NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully launched on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos. This mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free! Hard work rarely speaks for itself. When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech). That plan stalled my career for about five years. I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role. So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?” Honestly, it never occurred to me.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing. A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse. In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out. “It will.

URL: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/11/were-asking-appeals-court-require-warrant-alpr-searches

Today, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant, a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr.

### Why Fewer People Are Challenging Bad Patents
Source: Electronic Frontier Foundation
Published: 2026-11-09 21:40 UTC
URL: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/11/why-fewer-people-are-challenging-bad-patents
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Electronic Frontier Foundation [technology_politics] https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/11/why-fewer-people-are-challenging-bad-patents

The number of petitions being filed at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) has collapsed. That’s not reason for celebration. The PTAB is an important line of defense against low-quality software patents being used in lawsuits against people and companies. The drop didn’t happen because suddenly patents have become higher quality. It’s simply because USPTO leadership is increasingly refusing to consider good challenges to patents, for reasons unrelated to the merits. The process has become so unreliable that many would-be patent challengers aren’t even trying. Inter partes review (IPR) is a process that allows people to challenge patents at the Patent Office, rather than having to fight an expensive lawsuit in federal court. It’s one of the most important ways to get bad patents out of the system. In the third quarter of 2026, July through September, only 97 IPR petitions were filed at the PTAB, compared to 327 petitions during the same period in 2025.

For the past two decades, the U.S. Supreme Court has been slowly weakening the Alien Tort Statute (ATS), a key human rights law that allows foreign nationals to sue persons or entities in civil court for harms resulting from violations of international law. The court’s recent ruling in Cisco Systems, Inc. v. Doe I dealt the law a final blow, foreclosing—absent new legislation by Congress—any future ability by plaintiffs to use the law to hold technology companies accountable for aiding and abetting human rights abuses. EFF filed multiple amicus briefs in the case, including most recently in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court Rejected New Causes of Action Under the ATS The ATS was passed by the very first Congress in 1789 and in just a few words gives U.S. federal courts jurisdiction to hear civil claims brought by foreign nationals against defendants who violated “the law of nations or a treaty of the United States." There has been a longstanding question about what counts as a valid civil claim under “the law of nations.” In Sosa v.

Attribution: Electronic Frontier Foundation [technology_politics] https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/11/google-forcing-ai-students-bs

Google is rightfully facing blowback for forcing K-12 schools to enable AI if they wanted to keep using Google search. The company quickly backtracked and decoupled and turned off the services by default, but made it clear search will continue to be just another AI chatbot. This mandate forces an ultimatum on educators: accept generative AI or de-google your school. Students, teachers, and parents across the U.S. are now years into an argument about how schools should respond to the growth of AI-enabled tools. Google decided to skip this debate and take this choice from schools. In August it activated AI chatbot Gemini for 150 million K-12 students on Google Classroom, leaving educators scrambling to respond. A few months later, Google introduced a new way to turn it off — but now administrators would also be turning off Google search. Google walked this back somewhat, clarifying that Gemini, Gemini notebook, and Search will have their own controls and will be off by default.

What does the digital future look like? Who gets to imagine it, shape it, and make it real? Building a freer, more inclusive digital age requires not only challenging systems of surveillance and control, but also making space for creativity, community, and radical imagination. That's why earlier this year with the queer arts collective, we put out a call for submissions inviting people to explore the intersections of technology, identity, and digital liberation—whether that involved pointing the lens towards an underrepresented issue in digital justice efforts; sharing personal accounts of joy, pleasure, or sorrow under surveillance; or painting wide imaginations for our communities using technology for good instead of carcerality and doom. And we’re excited to share that the project is now live! Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures explores a digital world that dreams wilder and exists louder. Seven artists share their visions of digital liberation, spanning from early internet-coded yearning to escapist steamy chat rooms and seed-laced battle suits for revolution.

This is fascinating: The video describes a technique that can reveal where an otherwise unidentifiable recording was made by analyzing its audio for the faint sounds of passing aircraft. The technique is both fascinating and frightening. It works by looking at Doppler curves, which plot the way a plane’s sound changes as it passes overhead because of the Doppler effect. This is the same familiar Doppler effect that causes the frequency of a siren to rise as it approaches and then fall as it passes by and moves away. More generally, it’s the phenomenon whereby the frequency of a wave perceived by an observer changes when the observer and the source of the wave are moving in relation to one another...

Image: Low-tech Magazine Volume IV (2022-2026). Photo: Juliette Demaret. Low-tech Magazine presents the fourth volume in the chronological book series. It contains twenty articles that were published online between 2022 and 2026. Three earlier volumes collect articles written and published online between 2007 and 2021, which are also bundled in the “Compressed Edition”. This new volume is a bit different from the earlier books: eight of the articles are DIY guides or manuals, and we have grouped them together in the second part of the book. This volume covers the period that Marie Verdeil joined Low-tech Magazine, which partly shifted the focus from writing articles to building prototypes inspired by historical research. These prototypes also led us to conduct workshops in universities and participate in museum exhibitions. As is the case with all of our books, the articles have been edited and improved compared to the original web versions. Some articles gained extra or better images.

### Rediscovering the Handcart
Source: Low-Tech Magazine
Published: 2026-04-22 00:00 UTC
URL: https://solar.lowtechmagazine.com/2026/04/rediscovering-the-handcart/
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R3 · P4 · culture_probe
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Low-Tech Magazine [tools_workshop] https://solar.lowtechmagazine.com/2026/04/rediscovering-the-handcart/

Image: The handcart, equipped with a sail. Photo by Kris De Decker. The human-powered handcart is the oldest of vehicles, and it will likely be the last one around in the future. Of all vehicles, it’s the cheapest and least complex to build and use. It offers a large advantage over carrying a load on your back or dragging it over the ground - the even older concept of the sled. On the other hand, the handcart is cheaper and easier to use than the animal-powered cart. Oxen and donkeys eat more than humans, and they have their own will, which can work against the driver. Like any other wheeled vehicle, the handcart requires roads to drive on. This infrastructure has not always been available anywhere or at any time in history. For example, in medieval Europe, porters and pack animals were more common than handcarts because of poor roads. 1 In the West, the handcart only reached its heyday during the first decades of the Industrial Revolution, when it connected fast-growing cities to train stations and harbors.

Published: 2026-03-30 00:00 UTC

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Low-Tech Magazine [tools_workshop] https://solar.lowtechmagazine.com/2026/03/low-tech-magazine-the-uncompressed-book-series/

Image: The redesigned and revised chronological book edition. Photo: Marie Verdeil. Between 2019 and 2021, Low-tech Magazine published three books containing selections of articles from the website, spanning 14 years (2007-2021). In 2024, we launched the “compressed edition”, which squeezes the article catalog of the three-volume book series into just one book of 620 pages. We did this by switching to a smaller font size, downsizing most images, and opting for a two-column layout. I rewrote some articles, especially older ones, resulting not only in fewer pages but also in better articles. This revised edition of the original, “uncompressed” series is based on the edits made for the compressed edition. However, we increased the font and image sizes and returned to a one-column layout for improved reading comfort. The book design is a collaborative effort by Laia Comellas, Marie Verdeil, and Johanna Gratzer. Marie Verdeil made the covers, Vaiva Vinskaitė did the typesetting. ### Hackers, Forklifts, and Other Things Manufacturers Blame on Repair
Source: Repair.org
Published: 2026-05-11 18:06 UTC
URL: https://www.repair.org/blog/2026/5/11/manufacturers-have-a-new-argument-against-repair-everyone-else-is-too-dangerous
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R3 · P4 · culture_probe
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Repair.org [repair_maintenance] https://www.repair.org/blog/2026/5/11/manufacturers-have-a-new-argument-against-repair-everyone-else-is-too-dangerous

When lawmakers consider Right to Repair, manufacturers and their trade groups usually show up with the same script. They support repair, of course. They support consumer choice, naturally. They support small businesses, safety, sustainability, affordability, resilience, and probably puppies. They just oppose the actual law that would make repair possible. That script is on full display in Alaska, where HB 162 would give Alaskans more practical access to the parts, tools, and information needed to fix the products they own. And the opposition testimony has been revealing. Not because the arguments are new, but because they are so familiar, so exaggerated, and so openly hostile to the basic idea that anyone outside a manufacturer-controlled network can be trusted to repair anything. The message from industry is clear: repair is fine, as long as manufacturers get to decide who repairs, what gets repaired, when repair happens, and how much control they keep after the sale. That is not repair freedom. That is a service monopoly with better lighting.

### Cisco Is Hiding Its Repair Monopoly Behind “Security”
Source: Repair.org
Published: 2026-05-04 16:20 UTC
URL: https://www.repair.org/blog/2026/5/4/cisco-is-hiding-its-repair-monopoly-behind-security
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R3 · P4 · culture_probe
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Repair.org [repair_maintenance] https://www.repair.org/blog/2026/5/4/cisco-is-hiding-its-repair-monopoly-behind-security

It took years of pressure, but consumers and advocates forced Apple to let people fix their own phones. That fight is not over. It just moved. Now the targets include everything from McFlurry machines to John Deere tractors to enterprise hardware from Cisco Systems. And right now, Cisco is leading the pack in the race to be the least repair-friendly major OEM. Over the past two weeks in Colorado, Cisco, IBM, and Hewlett-Packard Enterprise helped unleash more than 20 lobbying firms to kill the right to repair for businesses and government. Their argument was simple. If you do not use OEM parts, you are putting national security at risk. This is not just wrong. It is fiction. Since the first right to repair bill in 2014, not a single real-world example has been produced to support this claim. Not one. No breach. No incident. No evidence. Just hypotheticals dressed up as policy. Instead, we get scenarios that sound like action movies, not reality. They also tried to argue that repair should be restricted for equipment used in nuclear facilities and other sensitive environments.

### A Manufacturer’s Guide to Right to Repair Compliance
Source: Repair.org
Published: 2025-10-18 13:20 UTC
URL: https://www.repair.org/blog/2025/10/18/a-manufacturers-guide-to-right-to-repair-compliance
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R3 · P4 · culture_probe

Attribution: Repair.org [repair_maintenance] https://www.repair.org/blog/2025/10/18/a-manufacturers-guide-to-right-to-repair-compliance

Overview: The New Reality of Repair With Right to Repair laws now active in states representing over a third of the U.S. market, non-compliance is no longer a viable option. For manufacturers, this shift presents a critical choice: treat repair as a burdensome legal obligation or embrace it as a strategic opportunity to build customer loyalty, open new revenue streams, and enhance brand reputation. This guide provides a clear roadmap for navigating the new legal landscape. The Legal Foundation of Right to Repair Resistance to Right to Repair statutes has often been based on flawed legal arguments that have consistently proven ineffective. The legal framework supporting repair is built on long-standing principles: Basic Ownership Law (the First Sale Doctrine): Many manufacturers have attempted to maintain control over products post-sale through End-User License Agreements (EULAs). However, legal precedent is clear: the transfer of ownership is complete at the point of sale. The new owner assumes responsibility for the product’s safety, security, and privacy.

### The Repair Association Backs Military Right to Repair (S.2209)
Source: Repair.org
Published: 2025-07-21 17:57 UTC
URL: https://www.repair.org/blog/2025/7/21/the-repair-association-backs-military-right-to-repair-s2209
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R3 · P4 · culture_probe
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Repair.org [repair_maintenance] https://www.repair.org/blog/2025/7/21/the-repair-association-backs-military-right-to-repair-s2209

The fight for the Right to Repair has reached a critical milestone in Washington. The Senate Armed Services Committee is reviewing S.2209, a groundbreaking bill that would guarantee our military’s right to repair the equipment they purchase and rely on. Today, we submitted a letter to Chairman Roger Wicker, Ranking Member Jack Reed, Senator Tim Sheehy, Senator Elizabeth Warren, and all members of the committee, voicing our full support for S.2209. This legislation would eliminate unnecessary repair monopolies, ensuring our armed forces can fix critical equipment on their own terms. Why S.2209 Matters Our military is the largest buyer of tech-enabled products in the world—yet too often, it’s locked out of essential repairs because manufacturers withhold access to parts, tools, or diagnostic information. These restrictions slow down readiness, inflate costs, and undermine the very concept of ownership. Repair isn’t about copying designs or exposing trade secrets. It’s a fundamental right tied to ownership, and it’s essential for operational readiness.

### Celebrating 50 States on the Right to Repair
Source: Repair.org
Published: 2025-02-24 10:00 UTC
URL: https://www.repair.org/blog/2025/2/24/ptkkw1yziw8xv7u9iwhoohl42ojyvu
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R3 · P4 · culture_probe
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Repair.org [repair_maintenance] https://www.repair.org/blog/2025/2/24/ptkkw1yziw8xv7u9iwhoohl42ojyvu

As of last week, all 50 states are now actively participating in the fight for our collective right to repair. Notably, Wisconsin and New Mexico introduced repair legislation for the first time, filling the final gaps on our nationwide map. Meanwhile, states like New York, Oregon, and Minnesota continue to enhance their existing laws, marking steady progress across the country. Our signature color scheme of black, red, and white has traditionally been used to signal clear legislative action. However, with many states now expanding their laws, we are exploring new ways to visually represent these developments without sacrificing clarity. Legislators are finding encouragement in the legislative successes of other states. Bills that pass in one state often pave the way for similar actions in others. By leveraging our experience from over 300 individual legislative efforts, we have been able to guide bill sponsors and drafters in avoiding early pitfalls and loopholes.

### John Deere Reaps What They Sow
Source: Repair.org
Published: 2025-01-21 15:19 UTC
URL: https://www.repair.org/blog/2025/1/21/john-deere-reaps-what-they-sow
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R3 · P4 · culture_probe
Fetched: 2026-11-09 23:41 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Repair.org [repair_maintenance] https://www.repair.org/blog/2025/1/21/john-deere-reaps-what-they-sow

The recent news that the FTC and AGs from two farm states (IL and MN) have filed litigation against John Deere is a terrific step forward for Right to Repair laws already in effect or underway. Even the dissenting letters offered by two FTC commissioners support the Right to Repair but don’t like the timing of the filing, which is so close to a new administration in the White House. We understand the partisanship concerns, but there is no real excuse for a delay. John Deere has been dodging Right to Repair compliance for a decade in anticipation of actual enforcement being delayed or removed altogether. The FTC just laid down a marker that repair monopolies will be disbanded. Our organization, the Digital Right to Repair Coalition (aka repair.org) has been in the middle of this fight since our founding in 2013. We have worked tirelessly with legislators from both sides of the aisle to make sure that we can all fix our stuff. It’s our small “r” right to control the property we buy.
